claims.claim_vi: AOF uses write(2) and fdatasync(2); both can cause latency. With appendfsync no the only source is write(2); with everysec the fsync runs in another thread and Redis delays write(2) up to two seconds if an fsync is in progress, then writes anyway, which can cause latency; with always an fsync is done before replying.
claims.section: Latency due to AOF and disk I/O

claims.claim_vi: appendfsync always is very slow and very safe; everysec is the default and may lose one second of data; no leaves flushing to the OS, normally every 30 seconds on Linux.
claims.section: How durable is the append only file?

claims.claim_vi: redis.conf of 7.0.15 sets appendfsync everysec by default.
claims.verified_by: Read from a clone of redis/redis at tag 7.0.15 (commit f35f36a265403c07b119830aa4bb3b7d71653ec9).

claims.claim_vi: In Redis 7.0.15, flushAppendOnlyFile returns without writing while an everysec background fsync is in progress (for up to two seconds, then writes anyway), and beforeSleep then still sends pending replies; the buffered record is written in a later event-loop iteration. Under always, a write barrier keeps the reply until after the fsync.
claims.verified_by: Read from a clone of redis/redis at tag 7.0.15 (commit f35f36a265403c07b119830aa4bb3b7d71653ec9).

claims.claim_vi: With auto AOF rewrite off and 40 overwrites of 5 MiB values 50 ms apart (three runs per setting): AOF off, SET median about 6 ms and another client's PING p99 under 0.6 ms with no latency events; always, SET 34-36 ms, PING p99 29-32 ms, aof-write up to 31-69 ms and aof-fsync-always 9-19 ms; everysec, SET 27-34 ms, PING p99 22-29 ms, aof-write up to 29-60 ms; no, SET 28-31 ms, PING p99 22-26 ms, aof-write up to 30-46 ms. With one write every 0.5 s, aof-write still reached 28-31 ms in all three modes. A 5 MiB GET took about 3.5 ms.
claims.verified_by: Experiment run by the author on 2026-10-18 on one virtual machine: Redis 7.0.15 (Ubuntu package), ext4 on a virtual disk, raw RESP client in Python, latency-monitor-threshold 1, LATENCY LATEST and INFO commandstats read after each run; a separate Python process sent PING every millisecond. Numbers are from one machine.

claims.claim_vi: With auto AOF rewrite left on, fork and aof-write-active-child events also appeared; switching from always to everysec made small SETs faster (median about 0.2-0.3 ms versus 0.04 ms).
claims.verified_by: Experiment run by the author on 2026-10-18 on one virtual machine: same set-up, first runs with default auto-aof-rewrite settings and 100-byte SETs.

claims.claim_vi: AOF logs the received write commands. Since Redis 7.0 the AOF is a base file (an RDB- or AOF-format snapshot taken at the rewrite) plus incremental files; redis.conf of 7.0.15 sets aof-use-rdb-preamble yes, so the base file is RDB by default (confirmed with CONFIG GET). With AOF on and a 100,000-field hash (about 9 MB by MEMORY USAGE), one HSET of a small field grew the AOF by 52 bytes.
claims.verified_by: Read from a local clone of redis/docs at commit 3b030c7ef066c0bb7f88ddec02c784e49783b0f8, the head of its default branch when read on 2026-10-18 (a later change to that branch does not alter this URL). The HSET measurement was run by the author on 2026-10-18 on Redis 7.0.15 with auto AOF rewrite off.

claims.claim_vi: A big key is a key holding a lot of data; the three AOF modes are Always, EverySec and No; the source states that in EverySec and No modes big keys have no impact on the main thread.
claims.section: How do we analyze the impact of big keys?

design_notes_vi: Bốn bước của một lệnh ghi để thấy write và fsync là hai bước khác nhau, ba chế độ, và số đo. Bảng số đo đặt trong bài; hình chỉ nói hướng.
source_deviations: Source says big keys have no impact on the main thread in EverySec and No modes; Redis's latency documentation and the lesson's measurement both show the write(2) on the main thread still blocks it.
The lesson adds a measurement on Redis 7.0.15 and a way for the reader to repeat it.
The figure shows the reply waiting for fsync only under always; under everysec and no the reply does not wait for the disk, and other clients wait on the main-thread write.

The figure and text add the everysec branch: while a background fsync is running the write is postponed up to 2 s, the reply goes out first and the late write blocks whichever clients are served then (Redis 7.0.15 source).
The modes panel says everysec usually loses about one second of data in a crash, more when the write is postponed.
